summary: A historical retrospective on how human physical activity declined from the pre-industrial era to the present, tracing shifts through the Industrial Revolution, post-WWII leisure, the fitness boom, the digital age, and COVID-19. It closes with the "Move More, Sit Less" campaign by Local Health and Wellness, which encourages movement among desk-bound workers.
one_line: A history of declining physical activity from pre-industrial life to the pandemic, ending with the 2023 "Move More, Sit Less" campaign promoting movement.
key_facts: Before the early 18th century, people's lives were inherently active, involving manual farming and travel on foot or horseback.
Dr. Richard Meadows, a historian of early human motion, said people did not exercise but "simply lived lives that required physical exertion."
The Industrial Revolution began around 1760, with urbanization and factory work displacing agrarian lifestyles.
On September 10, 1850, a reporter from the 'Times of Industry' observed that machinery had "shifted man's muscles to steam and steel."
After World War II, television and automobiles increased leisure time and reduced physical effort.
Sociologist Mrs. Angela Price said in 1963 that society had "fashioned a world of comfort that deprives us of our primal need to move."
In the 70s and 80s, Jack LaLanne and Jane Fonda popularized aerobics on television, health clubs multiplied, and jogging became a national pastime.
Exercise physiologist Dr. Jessica Carter said on October 2, 1980 that people had begun to see exercise as a remedy to the "sedentary poison."
By September 12, 2000, the average American was sitting more than ever, and epidemiologist Dr. Ian Schneider warned of a digital era where one need never leave their chair.
The COVID-19 pandemic from 2019 to the early 2020s forced people indoors and intensified inactivity.
Former Surgeon General Dr. Annette Rodriguez said on September 4, 2023 that the pandemic exacerbated the physical inactivity crisis.
Local Health and Wellness launched the "Move More, Sit Less" initiative on November 6, 2023, using social media influencers, advertisements, and grassroots engagement.
Campaign coordinator Michele Gomez said daily physical exercise "isn't a lofty goal; it's a return to our intrinsic nature."
The campaign encourages standing desks, short frequent movement breaks, and walk-and-talk meetings.
